Icebergs as a Water Source
Pat Quilty explains why icebergs may yet alleviate
global water shortages
The idea of using icebergs as a water source has been
around for a long time but up until now has seemed
closer to science fiction than science fact. Iceberg
utilization has already begun on a small scale in the Northern Hemisphere, where it is
used in some drinks, and companies are already beginning to explore the concept
seriously. But how realistic is it to foresee a time when ice in areas such as the Antarctic,
Iceland or Greenland will be exploited more widely as a resource?
The world's human population of six billion uses approximately 3240km’ of water each
year from a total annual renewable resource of some 41,000km*. Antarctica, with about
30 million km®, contains 90% of the Earth's ice and 70% of its fresh water. It yields about
1250km*, one third of our annual global consumption, in the form of icebergs. With the
world population expected to double to about 10-12 billion in 50 years, and with
uncertainty about the impact of global climate change, pressure on the global water
inventory will grow significantly and will increase the need to begin using iceberg water
on a much larger scale.
The idea that icebergs could supply drinkable water was first discussed at an
international conference in Iowa in 1977 and there was a flurry of interest at the time.
Most interest was based on the idea of towing icebergs, but this was never considered
viable because of the high cost of fuel. But technological advances could change this in
the next 30-50 years, when icebergs may be used commercially as a water source. This
idea is being considered in many parts of the world, and particularly in Australia where
water supply is a constant problem.
In 1985 a report by a German company, Ingenieurburo fur Abfalltechnik (IA), came up
with a proposal to produce drinking water by wrapping small, flat-topped icebergs near
the Antarctic Peninsula in a ‘bag’. The company had developed and experimented with a
plastic film reinforced with a fibre web, and suggested that such a system would have
several advantages.
First they noted that relatively small icebergs (300,000 to one million tonnes) could be

The concept is basically simple and was used to wrap an iceberg of 3000 tonnes. The
plastic was in rolls two metres wide, which were unrolled and attached together at the
same time by welding them. As the sheets were welded, to make handling easier, they
were gathered into pleats, much like a fan, on a floating barge that was brought to the
upstream side of the iceberg. The plastic was then allowed to sink under its own weight
and drift under the iceberg. If the currents weren't strong enough the plastic was to be
pulled by cables. Once the underside of the iceberg was covered, tubes in the plastic
were inflated with air to make the plastic rise, excluding most seawater in the process.
Small-scale experiments have already been conducted using a German Antarctic research
vessel. These included allowing ice-water to remain in this plastic for several months at
sea in the cold Antarctic to determine whether the plastic would deteriorate. Apparently
it did not. The report considered that even if the bag were to let in up to 2.5% seawater it
would still provide useful water.
Covering the top of the iceberg was more difficult because friction made it impossible to
simply pull the plastic across the top of the iceberg. Instead, cables with air-filled rollers
to overcome friction were pulled across the top of the iceberg. Once the iceberg was
covered, the plastic was sealed and it was ready to be towed or carried by the current.
Once safely wrapped, an iceberg could theoretically be taken almost anywhere on Earth
utilizing ocean currents as the major transporting mechanism.
There is no doubt that increasing population, raised standards of living, increased energy
costs and global warming will make water more sought after in the future. The
advantage of using icebergs as a water source lies in the minimal impact on any
environment in the Antarctic, and in alleviating environmental problems at or near the
destination. This makes it likely that icebergs will become used as a water resource in
the lifetimes of our children or grandchildren. Hopefully, iceberg use will be restricted to
localities suffering from severe drought and will not be a matter of simple convenience.
